endorsements.title: Developing, purchasing, implementing and monitoring AI tools in radiology: practical considerations. A multi-society statement
endorsements.issuer: ACR, CAR, ESR, RANZCR, RSNA; Radiol Artif Intell 2024 (PMID 38251899, doi:10.1148/ryai.230513)
endorsements.quote: In communities where radiology services are scarce, the deployment of autonomous AI raises complex ethical questions. While autonomous AI can provide diagnostic insights in the absence of skilled radiologists, decisions made by AI systems could potentially lack nuanced human judgment. Striking a balance between accessible healthcare and maintaining diagnostic quality becomes a critical ethical concern.

evidence.title: A community-codesigned LLM-powered chatbot for primary care: a randomized controlled trial
evidence.outcome: Differential intervention benefit for rural vs urban participants
evidence.effect: Rural participants had smaller gains on all six metrics: awareness 0.53 vs 0.73, attention 0.36 vs 0.57, listenability 0.27 vs 0.47.
evidence.quote: Rural participants exhibited smaller improvements across all six evaluation metrics compared with their urban counterparts (Fig. 4a ), with the most notable disparities in awareness (rural 0.53 ± 0.06 versus urban 0.73 ± 0.08), attention (0.36 ± 0.05 versus 0.57 ± 0.07) and listenability (0.27 ± 0.05 versus 0.47 ± 0.06).

evidence.title: Automated Calls Added to SMS Reminders Reduce Missed Appointments among High-Risk Patients
evidence.venue: NEJM catalyst innovations in care delivery
evidence.outcome: Racial differences in appointment completion benefits
evidence.effect: Appointment completion rates increased most among Black patients, reducing a preexisting equity gap. Subgroup effect sizes were not reported.
evidence.quote: It also increased appointment completion rates the most among Black patients, helping to reduce a preexisting equity gap.

evidence.title: Closing the accessibility gap to mental health treatment with a conversational AI-enabled self-referral tool
evidence.outcome: Change in referrals by demographic subgroup after chatbot self-referral introduction versus matched comparator services
evidence.effect: Total referrals rose 15% vs 6% in matched services; increases were larger for non-binary (235%), bisexual (30%), and ethnic minority (31%) individuals.
evidence.quote: Importantly, the tool was particularly effective for minority groups, which included non-binary (235% increase), bisexual (30% increase), and ethnic minority individuals (31% increase).

evidence.title: Autonomous Artificial Intelligence Increases Access and Health Equity in Underserved Populations with Diabetes
evidence.outcome: Change in diabetic eye disease testing adherence by race at AI vs non-AI sites
evidence.effect: Black/African American adherence rose 11.9% at AI-switched sites vs fell 1.2% at non-AI sites; Asian vs Black gap shrank from 15.6% (61.1% vs 45.5%) to 3.5% by 2021.
evidence.quote: The adherence rate for Black/African Americans increased by 11.9% within AI-switched sites whereas it decreased by 1.2% within non-AI sites over the same time frame.

evidence.title: Autonomous artificial intelligence for diabetic eye disease increases access and health equity in underserved populations
evidence.outcome: Change in DED testing adherence by race across AI-switched vs non-AI sites
evidence.effect: Adherence for Black/African Americans rose 12.2 percentage points at AI-switched sites vs a 0.6% point decrease at non-AI sites (p<0.001); Asian–Black adherence gap shrank from 15.6% to 3.5%.
evidence.quote: Second, the adherence rate for Black/African Americans increased by 12.2 percentage points within AI-switched sites but decreased by 0.6% points within non-AI sites (p < 0.001), suggesting that autonomous AI deployment improved access to retinal evaluation for historically disadvantaged populations.

evidence.title: Autonomous AI for diabetic eye disease at primary care improves ophthalmic access for at-risk patients
evidence.outcome: Distribution of ophthalmic access by patient subgroup between AI and standard-of-care referral pathways
evidence.effect: AI referral pathway patients were more likely to be Black (p < 0.001) and have hypertension (p = 0.001); no difference in presenting BCVA between pathways.
evidence.quote: However, patients from the AI referral pathway were more likely to be Black (p < 0.001) and have hypertension (p = 0.001), suggesting that deployment of autonomous AI is associated with improved ophthalmic access for patients with a higher baseline risk for poor DED outcome before vision loss has occurred.

evidence.title: Increasing Use of a Postpartum and Newborn Chatbot among Birthing Individuals and Caregivers: Development and Implementation Study
evidence.outcome: Chatbot reach (opening) by race, insurance, prenatal care location
evidence.effect: Lower postpartum reach for Black (OR 0.73) vs White, public insurance (OR 0.72) vs private; newborn reach lower for Black (OR 0.61), public insurance (OR 0.63), FQHC prenatal care (OR 0.50)
evidence.quote: The odds of opening the postpartum chatbot were significantly lower for individuals identified in the EHR as Black (odds ratio [OR] 0.73, 95% CI 0.61- 0.88) compared to White individuals.
evidence.sample_unit: chatbot recipients (6505 birthing individuals and 7489 newborn caregivers)

evidence.title: Improving ART Retention Through Machine Learning–Guided Targeting of Interventions: A Monte Carlo Simulation Study in Lilongwe, Malawi

evidence.effect: Newly initiated: 43.0% to 58.9%; clinically unstable: 28.3% to 39.1%; adolescents: 34.3% to 45.6%, a more modest effect.

evidence.title: Connecting algorithmic fairness and fair outcomes in a sociotechnical simulation case study of AI-assisted healthcare
evidence.outcome: Fair distribution of AI-enabled care benefits when access barriers differ between groups
evidence.effect: Access barriers had greater impact on disparities than AI fairness; enforcing equalized odds reduced disparity ~12 per 100k vs ~57 per 100k with 93% screening access.

evidence.venue: Journal of managed care & specialty pharmacy

evidence.effect: Black (RRR 4.31; 95% CI 3.92-4.75) and Hispanic (RRR 2.28; 2.04-2.56) beneficiaries more likely included under hospitalization/ED scheme only vs total cost scheme only; Asian (RRR 0.24) and Other (RRR 0.43) less likely.

commentary.bottom_line: One randomized trial of an AI tool in 59,994 US patients reported subgroup results and found that appointment completion rose most among Black patients, but it did not report subgroup effect sizes and did not test equity assessment itself as an intervention. Hazard studies show that the reach and benefit of AI tools can differ by race, insurance, income, and rurality in either direction, which suggests these gaps become visible only when a system measures them.

perspectives.view: One randomized trial (n=59,994) tests the practice. It reported that appointment completion increased most among Black patients. The trial did not report subgroup effect sizes, and it evaluated an AI tool with subgroup analysis rather than the effect of a health system's equity assessment. Certainty is low because of indirectness, imprecision, and reliance on a single study.

Subgroup gaps appear in both directions. Postpartum chatbot reach was lower for Black patients (OR 0.73) and publicly insured patients (OR 0.72), and newborn reach was lower for patients who received prenatal care at an FQHC (OR 0.50). At AI eye screening sites, the Asian-Black adherence gap shrank from 15.6% to 3.5%. No study shows that assessment itself prevented harm.

Deployment studies suggest that subgroup analysis is feasible with routine data. In England, a chatbot self-referral study (n=129,400) compared demographic subgroups against matched services and found that ethnic minority referrals rose 31%. A pediatric chat study linked engagement to insurance and Social Vulnerability Index scores. None of these studies measured the staff time or data work that such assessments require.

The trial that tests the practice reported no Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy subgroups. Hazard studies that included such groups found lower engagement among Medicaid patients (OR 0.68) and smaller gains for rural participants in a Chinese trial that enrolled low-literacy and non-native-language participants, with listenability gains of 0.27 versus 0.47.

A simulation of 500,000 women per run found that access barriers affected disparities more than algorithm fairness did. Enforcing equalized odds reduced disparity by about 12 per 100,000, compared with about 57 per 100,000 with 93% screening access. This result suggests that assessments may need to cover access and uptake as well as model metrics. The finding comes from simulation.

Uptake varies before any benefit can occur. In a Spanish telemonitoring program, 40.2% of patients refused an AI virtual assistant, and refusal was associated with lower sociocultural level and fewer devices. In a US dermatology survey, Black race and darker skin tone predicted lower acceptance of AI-assisted care. Assessments that count only tool users may miss patients who declined.

commentary.research_gap: No study has tested whether a health system that routinely assesses AI access, benefit, and harm by subgroup achieves smaller disparities or fewer concentrated harms than one that does not. Trials of AI tools should report subgroup effect sizes with confidence intervals by insurance type, language, literacy, and safety-net site, and studies should measure the cost and staffing needed for ongoing equity monitoring.
commentary.underserved_note: The one study that tests the practice did not report Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy subgroups, so its findings do not extend to these groups. Several hazard studies did include them and found lower chatbot reach among publicly insured and FQHC patients and lower engagement among Medicaid patients, which suggests that assessment is least tested in the populations where gaps have been observed.
